source: Claude Doc 'Finance Den Ep. 1 — How Singapore Became Asia's Money Capital', Narration tab (rev 1)

sections.title: Trillion with a T
paragraphs: Every single day, about one and a half trillion US dollars' worth of currency changes hands in Singapore.
That's not a typo. Trillion, with a T. Every day. On an island you can drive across in under an hour.

Most people will tell you Singapore got rich because of its port. Ships, containers, location. And sure, the port matters. But that's not why billionaires from Jakarta, Beijing and Mumbai park their money here. It's not why Singapore is the third-biggest currency market on Earth, behind only London and New York.
The real story starts with a banker, a globe, and a gap in the world's clock. I'm Liam, welcome to the Den. Let's get into it.

sections.title: Pushed out, 1965
paragraphs: On the 9th of August 1965, Singapore became independent. Not because it fought for it, but because it was pushed out of Malaysia.

Think about the position it was in. No farmland worth mentioning. No oil. No minerals. It even had to buy much of its water from the neighbour that had just shown it the door. A small population, a harbour, and a lot of uncertainty.
So ask yourself: if you were handed that country, what would you sell?

Singapore's leaders had one asset they could actually grow: trust. If the world could trust Singapore with its goods, maybe the world could trust Singapore with its money. And money, unlike oil, doesn't need land.

sections.title: A gap in the world's clock
paragraphs: Here's the part most videos skip. In the late 1960s, Albert Winsemius, the Dutch economist advising Singapore's government, got talking with J. D. van Oenen, a vice-president at Bank of America's Singapore branch.

Van Oenen made his point with a globe. When markets in San Francisco close for the day, Europe hasn't opened yet. For a few hours, the world's money has nowhere to trade. Put a market in Singapore, and you fill that gap. The sun never sets on the trading day.
The idea went up to Finance Minister Hon Sui Sen, then to Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew. In 1968, Singapore launched what became known as the Asian Dollar Market.

Here's how it worked. Banks could open a special account, called an Asian Currency Unit, to take deposits and make loans in foreign currencies, mostly US dollars. That business was kept separate from the local economy. And the government taxed the income from it at a concessionary 10%.
In plain words: bring us your dollars, we'll keep it simple, and we'll keep the tax low.

At the same time, Singapore slowly removed exchange controls, the rules that stop money moving freely in and out. That's the opposite of what many newly independent countries were doing at the time. Most were building walls around their money. Singapore was taking them down.

sections.title: A referee and a boring currency
paragraphs: But a financial centre needs more than low taxes. It needs a referee. In 1971, Singapore created the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the MAS. It's the central bank and the financial regulator in one.

Then, in 1981, under its chairman Goh Keng Swee, MAS did something unusual. Most central banks fight inflation by moving interest rates. Singapore decided to manage its currency instead. It steers the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners' currencies, inside a band, and lets that band slowly crawl. Basket, band, crawl.

Why does that matter for money from abroad? Because if you're a foreign investor, your biggest fear in a small country is that its currency suddenly collapses. Singapore made its currency boring. And in finance, boring is beautiful.

Around the same time, Singapore set up two investment firms to manage the state's money: Temasek in 1974 and GIC in 1981. So the country wasn't just hosting other people's money. It was becoming a serious investor itself.
Step one: invite the money. Step two: prove you won't lose it.

sections.title: Barings, 1995
paragraphs: But trust can be lost in one trade. In 1992, a young British trader called Nick Leeson was sent to run Barings Bank's futures office in Singapore. Barings was Britain's oldest merchant bank.

Leeson was trading futures on Japan's stock market. When his bets went wrong, he hid the losses in an error account, an account meant for correcting small mistakes. Then he doubled down to win it back.
On the 17th of January 1995, a huge earthquake hit Japan around Kobe. The Japanese market fell, and Leeson's hidden bets fell with it.

The final bill: £827 million, about 1.4 billion US dollars. Around twice the trading capital Barings had available. On the 26th of February 1995, Britain's oldest merchant bank was declared insolvent. Leeson was sentenced to six and a half years in Singapore's Changi Prison.
One guy. One office. A centuries-old bank, gone.
You'd think that would scare money away from Singapore. Instead, it became a lesson the country took seriously: rules only work if someone is actually checking.

sections.title: Open, but careful
paragraphs: Then came 1997 and 1998, the Asian Financial Crisis. Currencies across the region collapsed. Banks failed. Many governments responded by closing up: more controls, more protection.

Singapore did the opposite. Its leaders decided to, in their own words, turn adversity into opportunity. They opened retail banking to foreign competition. They lifted limits on foreign ownership of insurers. They scrapped fixed brokerage fees. And they merged the stock exchange and the futures exchange into one: SGX, the Singapore Exchange.
When your neighbours lock their doors, you open yours. Guess where the money goes.

But, and this is the clever bit, Singapore opened up while staying strict. Its banks were made to hold more capital than international rules required. Liquidity rules came in before the rest of the world had them. Open, but careful. That combination is rare, and it's exactly what nervous money looks for.

sections.title: The numbers today
paragraphs: So where did all that get Singapore?

Number one: in April 2025, an average of 1.485 trillion US dollars in foreign exchange traded in Singapore every day. That's up 60% in three years, and about 12% of all the currency trading on the planet. Only the UK and the US are bigger.

Number two: in 2024, firms in Singapore managed about 6 trillion Singapore dollars, roughly 4.7 trillion US dollars, of assets. And here's the key detail: 77% of that money comes from outside Singapore.
Think about that. Most of the money in Singapore isn't Singaporean. That's the whole business model.
Number three: by the end of 2024, Singapore had about 2,000 single family offices. Those are private firms that manage one wealthy family's fortune. That was up from 1,650 just a few months earlier.
In the Global Financial Centres Index from September 2025, Singapore ranks fourth in the world, behind New York, London and Hong Kong, with only about a point separating each of the top four.

sections.title: The S$3 billion case
paragraphs: But when you're the place where the world's money feels safe, some of that money will be dirty.

In August 2023, Singapore police carried out raids across the city. The money-laundering case that followed grew to about 3 billion Singapore dollars in assets: luxury homes, cars, gold, cash. Ten foreign nationals were convicted and deported. In total, about 2.8 billion Singapore dollars was surrendered.

That's the trade-off every financial hub faces. The same openness that attracts honest investors also attracts people hiding money. And how a country handles that scandal decides whether the honest money stays.
Because being a safe place for money is the product. If dirty money gets comfortable, the product breaks.

sections.title: Lessons for Kigali
paragraphs: Now here's why I care about this story. Right now, cities across Africa and the Gulf are trying to copy Singapore's playbook. Kigali, Nairobi, Lagos, Dubai and others all want to be their region's money capital.

I'm recording this from Kigali. Rwanda has set up the Kigali International Financial Centre, and it wants to be a home for money moving in and out of Africa. The question is whether it can build the same things Singapore built: a real reason for money to come, a referee people trust, and a currency investors aren't afraid of.

Because look at what Singapore actually did. It didn't start with skyscrapers. It started with a reason for money to come: a gap in the world's clock. Then it built a referee people trusted, a currency that stayed boring, and rules strict enough to survive a Nick Leeson.
The lesson isn't "cut taxes and build towers." It's this: money goes where it's treated fairly, where it can move freely, and where it won't disappear overnight.

sections.title: The answer
paragraphs: So, was Singapore's wealth ever really about trade? The port got it started. But the money, trillions of it, came because a small country decided to become the world's most trusted place to keep it.

Next time in Money Cities, we're going to London, the city that still trades more currency than anywhere on Earth. If you want to see how money really moves around the world, subscribe, and I'll see you in the Den.
This video is for education only, not financial advice.
